intro: Beyond basic modular arithmetic and sieve techniques, these subtopics handle systems of modular constraints, huge-index linear recurrences, and divisor-structure counting arguments that show up constantly in Div. 1 E/F-level number theory problems.

subtopics.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
subtopics.theory:
The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) answers the question: given several congruences x ≡ r_1 (mod m_1), x ≡ r_2 (mod m_2), ..., x ≡ r_n (mod m_n), what values of x satisfy all of them simultaneously? The classical statement requires the moduli to be pairwise coprime: in that case there is a unique solution x modulo M = m_1 * m_2 * ... * m_n, constructed explicitly as x = sum_i r_i * M_i * y_i (mod M), where M_i = M / m_i and y_i is the modular inverse of M_i modulo m_i (guaranteed to exist because gcd(M_i, m_i) = 1 when the moduli are pairwise coprime). This construction is sometimes called Sun Tzu's theorem or Garner's algorithm, and it turns a system of n small congruences into a single congruence modulo the (much larger) product M — the standard reason CRT appears whenever a problem gives you "the answer modulo several different primes" and asks for the value modulo their product, or gives residues modulo a factored composite modulus (e.g. computing C(n,k) mod m for composite m by combining answers mod each prime power dividing m, as in the generalized-Lucas technique below).

The more generally useful (and more error-prone to implement) version drops the pairwise-coprime requirement entirely. Given x ≡ r1 (mod m1) and x ≡ r2 (mod m2) with possibly gcd(m1, m2) = g > 1, a common solution exists if and only if (r2 - r1) is divisible by g; when it exists, the merged congruence is x ≡ r (mod lcm(m1, m2)) for an explicitly computable r, found via the extended Euclidean algorithm applied to m1 and m2. The key identity: writing g = gcd(m1, m2) = p*m1 + q*m2 (Bezout coefficients from extended gcd), the merged solution is x = r1 + m1 * t, where t is chosen (mod m2/g) so that m1*t ≡ (r2 - r1) (mod m2), i.e. t ≡ ((r2-r1)/g) * p (mod m2/g). Because m1 and m2/g are not generally coprime to arbitrary intermediate products, every step of this computation must use 64-bit-safe or __int128 arithmetic to avoid silent overflow — this is by far the most common source of wrong-answer bugs in CRT implementations, since m1 * t and m1 * (m2/g) can each individually exceed a 32-bit or even a naive 64-bit intermediate before the final reduction mod lcm(m1,m2) brings the answer back down. General (non-coprime) CRT is applied iteratively: merge congruence 1 and 2 into a single merged congruence, then merge that result with congruence 3, and so on; if any merge step reports inconsistency, the whole system has no solution.

CRT shows up disguised in many contexts beyond "solve this system directly": periodicity problems where two independent cycles (e.g. two objects each cycling through states with different periods) must be combined into one master cycle length via lcm and phase-matched via CRT (as in problems about two processes that periodically return to matching states); the generalized Euler's theorem / "power tower mod m" technique, which recursively reduces the modulus via Euler's totient function and effectively needs CRT-style reasoning to combine the reduced results back together; and computing binomial coefficients modulo a non-prime-power or arbitrary composite modulus, where you factor the modulus into coprime prime-power pieces, solve independently modulo each piece (often via Lucas' theorem or its prime-power generalization), and CRT-combine the pieces into the final answer.
subtopics.recognition: You are given (or can derive) several independent congruences on the same unknown x with different moduli and need to find x itself, the smallest such x, or whether a consistent x exists at all. Also look for: two or more independent periodic processes whose combined period is a lcm and whose "alignment" needs an explicit residue (not just the period length); or a composite modulus that the problem intends you to factor into coprime pieces and solve separately.
subtopics.complexity: O(n log(max modulus)) to merge n congruences one at a time via the extended Euclidean algorithm (each merge is O(log(max modulus))); O(1) additional per-merge arithmetic with __int128 or manual overflow-safe multiplication.

examples.title: Reconstructing a Hidden Integer from Coprime Sensor Residues
examples.problem:
A hidden non-negative integer x is monitored by n independent sensors (2 <= n <= 15). Sensor i reports only the residue r_i = x mod m_i. The moduli m_1, ..., m_n are pairwise coprime (gcd(m_i, m_j) = 1 whenever i != j), and it is guaranteed that the product M = m_1 * m_2 * ... * m_n fits in a signed 64-bit integer. Given all n pairs (r_i, m_i), determine the unique integer x with 0 <= x < M consistent with every sensor's reading, together with M itself.

Input: n, then n lines each containing r_i and m_i.
Output: x and M, separated by a space.
examples.approach:
This is the textbook coprime-CRT construction (Sun Tzu / Garner). Compute M = product of all m_i. For each sensor i, compute M_i = M / m_i and its modular inverse y_i modulo m_i via the extended Euclidean algorithm (this inverse is guaranteed to exist because gcd(M_i, m_i) = 1, which follows from pairwise coprimality of all the moduli). The unique answer modulo M is x = (sum_i r_i * M_i * y_i) mod M.

Because M_i can be almost as large as M itself (up to ~9*10^18 given the stated bound), and it gets multiplied by r_i * y_i (each up to ~10^9), the running sum must be accumulated in __int128 to avoid overflow before the final reduction mod M brings the value back into 64-bit range. This was verified against the hand-computable case moduli {3,5,7} with residues {2,3,2}: x=23 is the unique value in [0,105) with 23 mod 3 = 2, 23 mod 5 = 3, 23 mod 7 = 2.

examples.title: Merging Possibly-Overlapping Modular Constraints (General CRT)
examples.problem:
You are given n congruences of the form x ≡ r_i (mod m_i) for 1 <= n <= 12, 1 <= m_i <= 10^9, where the moduli are NOT necessarily pairwise coprime (e.g. they could share common factors, as when two different constraints both happen to be multiples of a common divisor). Determine the smallest non-negative integer x that satisfies all n congruences simultaneously, or determine that no such x exists. It is guaranteed that if a solution exists, the least common multiple of all the m_i fits in a signed 64-bit integer.

Input: n, then n lines each containing r_i and m_i.
Output: the smallest non-negative x satisfying every congruence, or -1 if no such x exists.
examples.approach:
Use the general (non-coprime) CRT merge, applied iteratively left to right. Maintain a running merged congruence (curR, curM), initialized to (0, 1) (the trivial congruence "x ≡ 0 (mod 1)", satisfied by every x). For each new congruence (r_i, m_i), merge it with the running one via the extended Euclidean algorithm: let g = gcd(curM, m_i); the merge is only consistent if (r_i - curR) is divisible by g, in which case the merged modulus becomes lcm(curM, m_i) and the merged remainder is computed via the Bezout coefficients of curM and m_i (scaled and reduced modulo m_i/g, using __int128 throughout to avoid overflow in the intermediate product curM * t). If any merge step is inconsistent, output -1 immediately.

After merging all n congruences, curR is already the smallest non-negative solution modulo curM (the merge routine always normalizes its result into [0, curM)). This was verified two ways: the solvable chain (2 mod 4), (4 mod 6), (1 mod 15) merges step by step to (10 mod 12) then to (46 mod 60) — confirmed by direct check (46 mod 4 = 2, 46 mod 6 = 4, 46 mod 15 = 1); and the inconsistent pair (0 mod 4), (1 mod 2) correctly reports -1, since x ≡ 0 (mod 4) forces x ≡ 0 (mod 2), contradicting x ≡ 1 (mod 2).

subtopics.name: Matrix Exponentiation (Linear Recurrences)
subtopics.theory:
Any order-k LINEAR recurrence f(n) = c_1*f(n-1) + c_2*f(n-2) + ... + c_k*f(n-k) can be advanced by one step via a single matrix-vector multiplication: stack the k most recent values into a column vector v = [f(n-1), f(n-2), ..., f(n-k)]^T, and build the k x k companion transition matrix T whose first row is [c_1, c_2, ..., c_k] and whose remaining rows form a shifted identity (row i, for i >= 2, has a single 1 in column i-1, shifting each old value down one slot). Then T * v gives the next state vector [f(n), f(n-1), ..., f(n-k+1)]^T. Advancing N steps is then T^N * v_0, and T^N can be computed by repeated squaring in O(k^3 log N) time (each of the O(log N) squarings costs O(k^3) for the k x k matrix multiplication), which is exponentially faster than the O(N) naive DP whenever N is astronomically large (10^9 to 10^18) but k stays small (a handful to a few hundred).

The central skill in "hard" matrix-exponentiation problems is not the exponentiation itself but DERIVING the linear recurrence and the matrix that encodes it, which is frequently disguised. A classic pattern: counting the number of ways to build up a total of N units where each "move" contributes either 1 unit or a fixed larger amount M units gives the recurrence f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-M) (an order-M recurrence, not order-2!), requiring an M x M transition matrix even though the recurrence looks almost like Fibonacci. Another pattern multiplies rather than adds terms together (f(n) is a product of powers of previous terms rather than a sum) — there, you exponentiate the EXPONENT VECTOR via matrix power (since exponents add under multiplication, turning a multiplicative recurrence into a linear-additive one on the exponents), then reconstruct the actual value via a single modular exponentiation at the end. A third pattern has a transition matrix that is almost, but not quite, constant across steps (e.g. periodic with a few exceptional positions); there, you precompute the matrix product over one full period once, then patch in the handful of exceptional single-step matrices separately, so that only a poly-logarithmic number of matrix operations are needed even though the transition technically varies.

Implementation pitfalls specific to matrix exponentiation: always reduce every multiplication modulo the target modulus immediately (never let entries grow beyond ~10^18 before reducing, since two ~10^9 values multiplied already approach 64-bit overflow); handle the exponent N being smaller than k by falling back to plain iterative DP (matrix exponentiation is only needed once N exceeds the base case window you've precomputed directly); and be careful that the state vector ordering used to build T is consistent with the ordering used to extract the answer afterward (a very common off-by-one-position bug).
subtopics.recognition: The recurrence relating f(n) to a FIXED, small number of previous terms is linear (each previous term appears with a constant, n-independent coefficient, added together — not multiplied, and not through a data-dependent formula), and n itself can be astronomically large (10^9 up to 10^18), ruling out a plain O(n) DP table. If the recurrence order k is itself large (hundreds), matrix exponentiation's O(k^3 log n) can become the bottleneck, at which point polynomial-based methods (Kitamasa / Bostan-Mori, achieving O(k^2 log n) or better) become preferable — but matrix exponentiation remains the standard, simplest-to-implement tool whenever k is at most a few dozen.
subtopics.complexity: O(k^3 log n) time for a single query with recurrence order k and target index n; O(k^2) space for the transition matrix.

examples.title: Throwing Dice (order-6 linear recurrence)
examples.problem:
Count the number of distinct sequences of die throws (each throw shows a value from 1 to 6) whose values sum to exactly n, for n up to 10^18. Two sequences are different if they have a different length or differ in some position. Print the count modulo 10^9 + 7.

Input: a single integer n.
Output: the count of such sequences modulo 10^9 + 7.
examples.approach:
Let f(n) = number of throw-sequences summing to exactly n, with f(0) = 1 (the empty sequence, base case) and f(n) = 0 for n < 0. Conditioning on the value of the LAST throw (which can be any of 1..6, as long as it does not exceed the remaining sum) gives the order-6 linear recurrence f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) + f(n-3) + f(n-4) + f(n-5) + f(n-6) for n >= 1 (terms with negative index contribute 0). For n <= 6, compute f directly by unrolling this recurrence with the known base case. For n > 6, build the 6x6 companion transition matrix T (first row all 1s, sub-diagonal shifted identity below it), form the state vector [f(6), f(5), f(4), f(3), f(2), f(1)], and compute T^(n-6) applied to this state via fast matrix exponentiation, reading off the first coordinate as f(n).

Hand-verification: f(1)=1, f(2)=2, f(3)=4, f(4)=8, f(5)=16, f(6)=32 (each simply doubles while n <= 6, since every earlier f(i) for i<n contributes once), and f(7) = f(6)+f(5)+f(4)+f(3)+f(2)+f(1) = 32+16+8+4+2+1 = 63, matching this example's test case exactly (this is also the well-known CSES 'Throwing Dice' sample answer).

examples.title: Magic Gems (order-M composition-counting recurrence)
examples.problem:
You are constructing a sequence of "gems" to reach a total size of exactly N units, where N can be as large as 10^18. Each gem you place is EITHER an ordinary gem, contributing exactly 1 unit, OR a magic gem, which is split into exactly M unit pieces, contributing exactly M units (M is a fixed integer given in the input, 2 <= M <= 100). Count the number of distinct ORDERED sequences of gem choices that sum to exactly N units (two sequences differing in the order of gem types are counted separately). Print the answer modulo 10^9 + 7.

Input: two integers N and M.
Output: the count of valid sequences modulo 10^9 + 7.
examples.approach:
Let f(n) = number of ordered gem sequences summing to exactly n units. A sequence summing to n either ends with an ordinary gem (1 unit), in which case the rest sums to n-1, or ends with a magic gem (M units), in which case the rest sums to n-M. This gives the order-M linear recurrence f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-M) for n >= M, with base cases f(0) = 1 (empty sequence) and f(i) = 1 for 0 < i < M (the only way to reach a total less than M is to use i ordinary gems in a row — a single fixed sequence, since a magic gem alone would already overshoot).

Build the base state directly (f(0) through f(M)), then, for N > M, form the M x M transition matrix (row 0 has a 1 in column 0 and a 1 in column M-1, encoding f(i+1) = f(i) + f(i-M+1); remaining rows shift the state down by one) and raise it to the power N - M via fast matrix exponentiation applied to the state vector [f(M), f(M-1), ..., f(1)]. Hand-verified with M=3: the sequence f(0..10) = 1,1,1,2,3,4,6,9,13,19,28 was checked by direct recurrence unrolling (f(3)=f(2)+f(0)=1+1=2, f(4)=f(3)+f(1)=2+1=3, ..., f(10)=f(9)+f(7)=19+9=28), and the program reproduces f(10)=28 exactly via its matrix-exponentiation code path (since 10 > M=3, the matrix-power branch is actually exercised, not just the small-case fallback).

subtopics.name: Lucas' Theorem & Möbius Inversion
subtopics.theory:
LUCAS' THEOREM answers: what is C(n, k) mod p, for a PRIME p, when n and k are far too large to build a factorial table up to n (n can be up to 10^18) but p itself is small enough (typically up to ~10^6) to build a factorial table up to p? Write n and k in base p as n = n_m n_{m-1} ... n_1 n_0 and k = k_m k_{m-1} ... k_1 k_0 (padding with leading zero digits as needed so both have the same number of base-p digits). Lucas' theorem states C(n, k) mod p = product over i of C(n_i, k_i) mod p, where each C(n_i, k_i) is an ordinary, SMALL binomial coefficient (since 0 <= n_i, k_i < p, it can be looked up from a factorial table of size p) — and crucially, if k_i > n_i for ANY digit position i, the entire product (and hence C(n,k) mod p) is 0. This reduces an intractably large binomial coefficient to O(log_p n) small lookups. The theorem generalizes further to PRIME-POWER moduli p^e (via Andrew Granville's/Kummer's extension, which tracks carries in base-p addition) and then to ARBITRARY composite moduli m by factoring m into coprime prime-power pieces, solving each piece with the prime-power generalization, and combining the pieces with the Chinese Remainder Theorem described above — this three-layer combination (Lucas + prime-power extension + CRT) is the standard technique for "C(n,k) mod m for arbitrary m" problems, and is one of the more advanced set-piece techniques in competitive number theory (real standalone practice problems requiring exactly this combination are rare outside ICPC-style problem sets, since the technique usually appears folded into a larger combinatorics problem).

MÖBIUS INVERSION is a different (and, in practice, far more frequently tested) tool for counting problems phrased in terms of gcd or divisibility. The Möbius function μ(d) is defined as μ(1)=1; μ(d)=0 if d has any squared prime factor; and μ(d)=(-1)^r if d is a product of r DISTINCT primes. Its key property is that sum_{d | n} μ(d) equals 1 if n=1 and 0 otherwise — which is exactly the indicator you need to turn "count things whose gcd is EXACTLY 1" (hard to count directly, because of double-subtraction across overlapping multiples) into "a signed sum, over all d, of (count of things where every element is divisible by d)" (each term easy to count directly). Concretely, if you want to count objects with gcd exactly g, you instead compute, for every multiple d of g, the (easy) count of objects where g*d divides every relevant value, and combine these easy counts with μ(d) coefficients: answer(gcd = g) = sum_{d=1}^{∞} μ(d) * (count of objects where g*d divides everything). This is the Mobius-inversion analogue of inclusion-exclusion over the divisor lattice, and the μ values themselves are computed once via a linear (or O(n log log n)) sieve, exactly like the sieve of Eratosthenes but tracking each number's smallest prime factor to detect repeated prime factors.

The most common concrete pattern: count PAIRS (or subsets, or sequences) of numbers from an array that are pairwise coprime (gcd = 1). Compute cnt[d] = number of array elements divisible by d (via a divisor-sieve pass, itself O(V log V) for values up to V), then the answer is sum_d μ(d) * g(cnt[d]), where g(c) is whatever "easy" count applies to c objects (C(c,2) for pairs, 2^c - 1 for non-empty subsets, etc.). This single template solves a large family of "count structures with gcd exactly 1" problems, and extends naturally to "gcd exactly equal to some specific value G" by first dividing every array element by G (discarding those not divisible by G) and then solving the gcd-exactly-1 version on the reduced array.
subtopics.recognition: Lucas' theorem: you need C(n, k) mod p for a PRIME (or prime-power, or arbitrary) modulus p, where n and/or k are too large for a direct factorial table but p is small. Mobius inversion: the problem talks about counting tuples/subsets/pairs/sequences with a gcd (or lcm) constraint — especially "gcd exactly 1" or "pairwise coprime" — and a naive count would double-count or under-count due to overlapping multiples; especially recognizable when an easier "count things where d divides everything" sub-count is easy to compute for every d.
subtopics.complexity: Lucas' theorem: O(p) preprocessing (factorial table up to p) plus O(log_p n) per query. Möbius inversion: O(V log log V) to sieve μ up to the value bound V, O(V log V) to compute all the divisor counts cnt[d], and O(V) to combine them into the final answer.

examples.title: Binomial Coefficient Modulo a Small Prime, Huge n and k (Lucas' Theorem)
examples.problem:
Given three integers n, k, p where 0 <= k <= n <= 10^18 and p is a PRIME with 2 <= p <= 10^6, compute C(n, k) mod p (the binomial coefficient "n choose k", reduced modulo p).

Input: n, k, and p on one line.
Output: C(n, k) mod p.
examples.approach:
Direct application of Lucas' theorem. First, precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo p for all values 0..p-1 (using Fermat's little theorem for the modular inverse of (p-1)!, then working backward to fill in every inverse factorial in O(p) total). Define smallComb(a, b) for 0 <= a, b < p as fact[a] * invfact[b] * invfact[a-b] mod p (0 if b > a).

Then recursively peel off the least-significant base-p digit of n and k: lucas(n, k) = smallComb(n mod p, k mod p) * lucas(n/p, k/p), with the base case lucas(0, 0) = 1 (and lucas(n,0) = 1 for any remaining n, handled by the k==0 early return). If at any digit position k mod p exceeds n mod p, smallComb returns 0 immediately, which propagates to make the whole product 0 — correctly capturing that no valid "carry-free" combination exists at that digit (Kummer's theorem interpretation).

Hand-verified: C(10,2) = 45. In base 7, 10 = (1,3)_7 and 2 = (0,2)_7. Lucas gives C(3,2) * C(1,0) mod 7 = 3 * 1 = 3, and indeed 45 mod 7 = 3 (45 = 6*7 + 3), confirming the implementation.

examples.title: Counting Coprime Pairs (Möbius Inversion Sieve)
examples.problem:
Given an array of n positive integers (1 <= n <= 2*10^5, each value up to 10^6), count the number of PAIRS of indices (i, j) with i < j such that gcd(a_i, a_j) = 1 (the two chosen elements are coprime).

Input: n, then n integers a_1..a_n.
Output: the number of coprime pairs.
examples.approach:
Direct application of the Mobius-inversion counting template. First sieve the Mobius function μ(d) for all d up to the maximum array value, using a smallest-prime-factor sieve (mu[1]=1; for composite/prime i, if i's smallest-prime-factor divides i/spf[i] again — i.e. i has a repeated prime factor — mu[i]=0, otherwise mu[i] = -mu[i/spf[i]]).

Next compute cnt[d] = number of array elements divisible by d, for every d from 1 up to the max value, via a harmonic-sum divisor pass (for each d, sum the frequency of every multiple of d that appears in the array) — this costs O(V log V) where V is the max value, since it is exactly the same summation pattern as a sieve of Eratosthenes. Finally, the number of coprime pairs is sum_d μ(d) * C(cnt[d], 2): for each d, C(cnt[d], 2) counts all pairs where BOTH elements are divisible by d (i.e., pairs whose gcd is a multiple of d), and the Mobius-weighted sum over all d cancels out every pair whose gcd is greater than 1, leaving exactly the pairs with gcd exactly 1.

Verified by brute force (checking gcd of every pair directly) against several arrays, including this example's array [2,3,4,6,9]: the coprime pairs are (2,3), (2,9), (3,4), and (4,9) — 4 pairs total (every other pair shares a common factor: (2,4),(2,6),(4,6) share 2, and (3,6),(3,9),(6,9) share 3) — matching both the brute-force cross-check and the Mobius-sieve program's output.
